Reubenites
ROO-ben-ites
n. pl.
The descendants of Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn by Leah, whose name means see, a son. Firstborn by birth and disinherited by conduct, Reuben’s children settled the high pastureland east of Jordan and were the first tribe of Israel carried into captivity.

Biblical Definition

The Reubenites are the children of Israel’s firstborn, and their whole history is governed by a sentence spoken over their father on Jacob’s deathbed: Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father’s bed (Genesis 49:4). The birthright passed to Joseph’s sons, the priesthood to Levi, the sceptre to Judah. When Israel reached the plains of Moab, the Reubenites and the Gadites saw that the land of Jazer and Gilead was good for cattle and asked to be settled there: bring us not over Jordan (Numbers 32:5). Moses met the request with the question every generation should be asked — Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here? — and with the warning be sure your sin will find you out. They agreed to cross armed before their brethren and did so, and the land east of Jordan was theirs (Deuteronomy 3:12). But the choice had a long shadow. They built the great altar Ed by Jordan because they feared their children would one day be told What have ye to do with the LORD God of Israel? (Joshua 22:24). Their fear was not idle: the eastern tribes were the first to be swept away, when the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria… and he carried them away, even the Reubenites (1 Chronicles 5:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no REUBENITE entry. The name Reuben is Hebrew, see, a son, from Leah’s cry at his birth (Genesis 29:32), and the gentilic follows the ordinary Hebrew formation.

expand to see more

REUBENITE, n. — A descendant of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob; one of the tribe settled east of Jordan.

Genesis 29:32 explains the name: She called his name Reuben: for she said, Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction.

The tribe’s inheritance lay from the Arnon northward through the plain country (Deuteronomy 3:12, 16).

Bezer in the wilderness was their city of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8).

Webster 1828 does not carry biblical gentilics of this kind; the sense is fixed by Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Chronicles.

Key Scripture

Genesis 49:4 — "Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father’s bed; then defiledst thou it: he went up to my couch."

Numbers 32:6 — "And Moses said unto the children of Gad and to the children of Reuben, Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here?"

Numbers 32:23 — "But if ye will not do so, behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out."

Deuteronomy 3:12 — "And this land, which we possessed at that time, from Aroer, which is by the river Arnon, and half mount Gilead, and the cities thereof, gave I unto the Reubenites and to the Gadites."

1 Chronicles 5:26 — "And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day."

Modern Corruption

Numbers 32:23 is quoted constantly and almost always as a threat of exposure — the sin that will be found out. Moses is saying something graver: the sin itself will hunt the sinner down.

expand to see more

Be sure your sin will find you out is not a warning that someone will discover what you did. The Hebrew has the sin as the subject and the sinner as the object; it comes after him. That is why the phrase stands where it does, in a negotiation about settling short of the promised inheritance. Reuben and Gad did keep their word and cross armed; the sin Moses feared was not merely broken promise but the choice of good pasture over the land God had given, and that choice found them out four centuries later on the road to Halah and Habor. Sin is not chiefly dangerous because it may be reported. It is dangerous because it pursues, and because the pursuit is often generational and slow.

The second matter is the tribe’s founding disqualification. Reuben was the firstborn and lost the birthright by an act of sexual sin against his father’s household, and Jacob names it on his deathbed without euphemism. He is also the brother who tried to save Joseph from the pit and who offered his own two sons as surety for Benjamin — a man of real impulses and no stability. Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel. Scripture’s estimate of such a character is not that he lacked sincerity but that he lacked constancy, and constancy is what a firstborn must have. The New Testament word for it is steadfastness, and James applies the same figure to the doubting man, who is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Reuben (H7205), see, a son, from ra’ah to see and ben a son; the gentilic is Reubeni (H7206).

expand to see more

Hebrew Reuben (H7205) — Reuben; Leah’s firstborn, named at Genesis 29:32.

Hebrew Reubeni (H7206) — Reubenite; the gentilic used from Numbers 26:7 through 1 Chronicles.

Hebrew pachaz (H6349) — unbridled, wanton, unstable; the word behind unstable as water (Genesis 49:4).

Hebrew Ed — witness; the name given the altar by Jordan (Joshua 22:34), for it shall be a witness between us.

Hebrew Betser (H1221) — Bezer; the Reubenite city of refuge in the wilderness plain (Deuteronomy 4:43).

Usage

"Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here? (Numbers 32:6) — Moses’ question to a tribe that wanted to settle early."

"Be sure your sin will find you out (Numbers 32:23) — the sin, not the rumour, does the finding."

"He carried them away, even the Reubenites (1 Chronicles 5:26) — the first of Israel to go into exile."
